analysis.investment_thesis: Lloyds Engineering is a project-based industrial machinery company trading at an absurd 48x P/E — far outside the 12-20x I demand — with ROCE of just 9.8% and negative free cash flow in 3 of the last 4 years. This is a cyclical capital goods business masquerading as a compounder, and I want no part of it at this price.
key_strengths: Low debt — D/E of 0.16 is the one genuinely clean metric here
Operating margin of 17% is above-average for the sector
Revenue scaled 17x in 3 years (₹50 Cr → ₹846 Cr) indicating real order wins
key_risks: Valuation is punishing — P/E 48x, EV/EBITDA 48x for a cyclical project business is indefensible
Promoter holding at 41.9% is well below my 55% floor — skin in the game is inadequate
OCF was negative for 3 of 4 years; the 2025 positive ₹158 Cr is one data point, not a track record
red_flags: ROCE of only 9.8% — the business destroys capital on a risk-adjusted basis despite rising profits
Equity nearly tripled in one year (₹411 Cr → ₹1,188 Cr) — heavy dilution to fund growth, not organic compounding
Revenue CAGR of 157% is project-driven, lumpy, and almost certainly unsustainable — I distrust explosive growth
No dividend — consistent with a capital-hungry business, not a quality compounder
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Lloyds Engineering fails almost every criterion I use. It is an industrial project contractor — hydrocarbon, steel, nuclear, port equipment — deeply cyclical, dependent on government and PSU capex cycles, and structurally the opposite of the predictable consumer businesses I understand and trust. The financials look dramatic on the surface: revenue up 17x in three years. But this is order-book execution, not recurring demand. When the order cycle turns, margins and revenues will revert, and shareholders holding at 48x P/E will be badly hurt.

The capital quality is poor. ROCE of 9.8% means the business earns less than my cost of capital on deployed assets. Free cash flow was negative for three consecutive years — the company consumed ₹163 Cr of cash while reporting profits. The 2025 turnaround to ₹92 Cr FCF is encouraging but one year of data. The equity base tripled in FY25, strongly suggesting a large equity raise to fund working capital or acquisitions — dilution is not compounding. At ₹8,234 Cr market cap on ₹105 Cr net profit, the market is pricing in flawless execution for years ahead. I built DMart by being conservative when others were optimistic. Here, I see hype, not a business I can hold for twenty years.
